existing_incident_edges.relationship: 'Limited identities': the regional, ethnic and class identities Canadians have, proposed as the place where 'Canadianism' might be found (1967), a phrase Careless made a programme (1969)
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Cook's own text, 'Canadian Centennial Cerebrations', International Journal 22:4 (1967), pp. 659–663: the opening, read in the OpenAlex text of the article, attacks Canadian Dimension's 'Open Letter to Canadian Nationalists', likens it to Canada First's 1874 manifesto and asks 'Who says Canadian nationalism is difficult to define? Jobs!' (p. 659). The limited-identities sentence was not read on Cook's page; Buckner quotes it (2000, p. 4): 'Perhaps instead of constantly deploring our lack of identity, we should attempt to understand and explain the regional, ethnic and class identities that we do have. It might just be that it is in these limited identities that “Canadianism” is found'. Taken up: Careless (CHR 1969; unread here, quoted by Buckner, p. 4) held that the 'Canadian experience' must be 'discerned and defined' through the 'limited identities of region, culture and class referred to by Professor Cook'. Buckner (p. 5) writes that 'Cook and Careless' embraced the concept partly in response to Quebec separatism, quoting Cook's 1970 essay as reprinted in The Maple Leaf Forever (p. 213): 'Nationalism by nature tends strongly to centralism and uniformity: Canada is by nature federal, sectional and pluralist'; 'historians in Atlantic Canada eagerly espoused the concept of “limited identities”, but their motivations were rather different' (p. 5). In period, Buckner's 1988 abstract (recorded in cdng_buckner_1988, not re-read) calls it 'the catch phrase of the Canadian historical profession in the 1960s' and judges it 'premature to abandon'. Criticism: Reid (1987, opening, recorded in cdng_reid_1987) notes that during the 1980s 'concern has increasingly been expressed that fragmentation has been the result'; Gauvreau (1991, p. 164 n. 10) writes that limited identities 'has underwritten much of the “new social history”', which, like the older national history, 'marginalizes religious history'; Buckner (2000, p. 12) writes 'I think it implied to Cook and Careless' that national identity was the sum of component identities, calls that idea 'nonsensical', and argues that 'All identities are socially constructed'. Influence rather than contribution: Cook named the identities but wrote no regional history, and later questioned region as a unit of analysis (edge 2). The roster row calls him a precursor.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Region questioned as a unit of analysis: regional history's strengths and weaknesses weighed (1977), and regions recast as provinces, 'a concept whose time has gone' (1983)
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Cook's own review essays in Acadiensis, read in full. 'The Burden of Regionalism' (7:1, Autumn 1977, pp. 110–115), reviewing Bercuson's Canada and the Burden of Unity among other books, notes 'the tendency to see regionalism as a virtue of Canadian life rather than an obstacle to Canadian unity' (p. 110). Bercuson's contributors assume 'that Canadian history is best understood from a regional perspective' (p. 112), but 'neither he nor anyone else in the book attempts to define the term' (p. 114); 'the “regional” approach to Canadian history, and to its discontents, has both strengths and weaknesses. The whole may not be greater than the parts, but it is at least the sum of them' (p. 115). 'Regionalism Unmasked' (13:1, Autumn 1983, pp. 137–142), reviewing L. D. McCann's Heartland and Hinterland (1982): 'I have begun to doubt seriously the existence of the phenomena we have for so long called regions, though regionalism as a rationalization of certain interests may have some reality' (p. 140); McCann's definition of region 'applies at least as well, and perhaps better, to a province as to a region. So why not call a region what it really is — a province' (p. 140); with Cole Harris's chapter, the book 'can really lead to no other conclusion than that, as a tool of analysis, “regionalism” is a concept whose time has gone' (p. 141). He qualifies this: 'Stripped of its rhetoric there remains with the regional approach, especially as practised by historical geographers, a legitimate preoccupation with some profoundly important aspects of our history: class, sex, family, ethnicity, for example' (p. 141), and he calls Wynn's Maritimes chapter 'the finest section of the book' (p. 138). In-period response: Buckner (2000, pp. 8–10) cites both reviews, though he dates the first 1974 and renders 'whose time is gone' where the 1983 page reads 'has gone'. He calls the fragmentation charge 'patently absurd, at least when applied to the Atlantic region' (p. 8) and holds that the Atlantic Provinces 'had legitimate grievances within Confederation' (p. 10), adding that he was 'initially ... as skeptical as Cook' (p. 10). The critique targets the regional framework and heartland–hinterland synthesis, not regional research as such.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: The Laurentian view criticised as regional rather than national, and the national school read as superseded (1977–83)
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Cook's own words, read in full. 'The Burden of Regionalism' (Acadiensis 7:1, 1977, p. 110): 'The so-called national schools have, in reality, had a rather obviously regional focus. Those who live in the Valley of the Fraser, the Red or the Restigouche can hardly accept the Laurentian view of Canadian history as “national”, unless, of course, they are content to be considered as “colonials” — a point made long ago by W. L. Morton. And the other nationalist themes fare little better.' 'Regionalism Unmasked' (Acadiensis 13:1, 1983, p. 137): 'the so-called “national” approach to the interpretation of the Canadian past has come under a destructive barrage of criticism' (the decade before it is garbled in the text layer); Berger's The Writing of Canadian History (1976) 'might be viewed as a lengthy epitaph on the headstone of the national school's grave'; Morton's 'Clio in Canada' (1946) 'made explicit what had long been implicit in the Innis-Creighton laurentian thesis: the metropolitan-hinterland relationship was not one of equality'. In-period context: Buckner (2000, pp. 4–5) sets limited identities (edge 1) against a post-war consensus of 'liberal nationalists such as A.R.M. Lower and Frank Underhill' and 'conservative nationalists such as Donald Creighton and C.P. Stacey' for whom the nation-state was the frame of reference. Limits: Cook credits the point to Morton; he co-wrote a Centenary Series volume (1974); and by Buckner's account (p. 8) he 'warned regional historians of the danger of ignoring the “national experience”' in 1977 ('The Golden Age of Canadian Historical Writing', Historical Reflections; unread here). The critique is of the Laurentian claim to speak for the nation, not of the staple studies' economics. edge_805 (cdn_regional → cdn_national_tradition, critique) carries the regional historians' version of the argument.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: The Regenerators: late Victorian social criticism read as the replacement of individual by social salvation, and the sacred becoming secular (1985)
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: The book is unread here: UTP and De Gruyter refused automated access, and the Internet Archive copy is borrow-only. Its contents are recorded in crr_cook_1985, including the closing chapter 'The Sacred Becomes the Secular'. Cook's words are known as quoted in in-period readings. Gauvreau (Acadiensis 1991, pp. 161–162) quotes 'the orthodox Christian preoccupation with man's salvation was gradually replaced by a concern for social salvation' and 'the substitution of theology, the science of religion, with sociology, the science of society' (Regenerators, p. 4); Christianity became 'less rather than more relevant' (p. 6); social conservatism 'went hand in hand with scientific conservatism, and both were founded on religious conservatism' (p. 12); and social regeneration became 'a substitute for the formidable labour of reformulating theological doctrine' (p. 229). Karr (Acadiensis 1989, p. 162) quotes that the book's subjects 'almost never alluded to the cultivation of a national sentiment' (p. 6). Gaffield's review (History: Reviews of New Books 14:5, 1986, p. 144; scanned page read by OCR and checked against the image) summarizes it: 'the call for social salvation emerged from a strong religious commitment but led to increasing secularization', and Cook 'treats religious thinking as an independent factor'. Contested in period. Gauvreau (1991) calls it 'important' but says it 'does not fully resist the temptation to view the 19th-century religious experience in relation to the 20th-century mind-set' (p. 161). He reads it as a '“neo-conservative” appropriation' of Allen's categories (p. 163); 'The appearance of The Regenerators in 1985 marked the beginning of the assault on Allen's position' (p. 163 n. 9). He adds that 'the emerging consensus seems to be away from “military metaphors” of the type employed by Cook' (p. 164). Van Die, he reports, 'ultimately accepts Cook's central thesis of the decline and irrelevance of Protestant religion, but does not agree with the conflict model' (p. 173). Marshall (CCHA Historical Studies 1993–94, web text without page numbers) names 'the secularization thesis outlined by McKillop, Cook, and Marshall' as Gauvreau's target and cites Regenerators pp. 228–32 (n. 6). Laverdure's 1998 review (crr_laverdure_1998, not re-read) says Christie and Gauvreau 'challenge the secularization thesis, most strongly advocated by Ramsay Cook … and David Marshall'. Karr (1989, p. 163 n. 21) finds 'an equally forceful Ontario bias' answering Allen's Western one. The name 'secularization thesis' is the critics', as the strand note says.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: An ecological interpretation of early Canadian history: contact as the interaction of ecologies, 'cabbages, at least as much as kings' (1990)
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Reuses the reading recorded on 2026-10-13 for the environment-family drafts (pe131_extras_cook_1990; canon-evidence-canada.md, text C1). It was not re-read for this entry because Project MUSE refused automated access. Cook's W. L. Morton Lecture (Trent, October 1990; JCS 25:4, 1990–91) starts from Morton's 1946 remark that history 'is concerned with ecology too' (p. 5): 'It is an insight which I would like to try to build upon' (p. 6). He marks a break with the staple historians: 'for this earlier generation of historians the exploitation of the environment was accepted as natural and necessary, even though excesses might be deplored' (pp. 6–7), while 'More recent environmental historians have a different focus. They are no longer much concerned with explaining the impact of the environment on man; it is the impact of man on nature that is at the centre of their work' (p. 7). Following Crosby, 'contact was even more significantly the interaction of different ecologies or environments' (p. 13). His conclusion: 'Cabbages, at least as much as kings, led to the transformation of the new world' (p. 15, as recorded in canon-evidence-canada.md; not in the source's verification note). In-period reading: Gauvreau (Acadiensis 1991, pp. 164–165 n. 12), arguing about Cook's religious history, called the lecture his 'recent “conversion experience” concerning the happy convergence of nature and culture'. Later reading, labelled: Wynn (2004, p. 33, recorded in pe131_extras_wynn_2004) quotes Cook's claim that Canadian historical writing 'has always been concerned with the environment' to describe Canadians who 'seemed to wonder what all the fuss was about'. A contribution, not a founding. edge_913 (harold_a_innis → environment) carries his continuity claim and Forkey's 1998 rejection of it; this edge carries his own ecological reading of contact.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Between 'nationalists' and 'limited identitarians': class, ethnicity and gender as what Canadians share, and identities as contingent and multiple (1993–2000)
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Cook's own words. 'The New History of Atlantic Canada' (Acadiensis 23:1, Autumn 1993, pp. 146–152, read in full) came between Bliss's 'Privatizing the Mind' (1991–92) and Granatstein's book (1998): 'one of the sweet ironies in the arid debate between “nationalists” and “limited identitarians” on historiography is that neither side appears to recognize that class, ethnicity and gender describe what groups of Canadians have in common, while “nationalism” most often provokes divisions — “regionalism”!' (p. 146). He holds that 'for all the emphasis on differences during recent decades, Canadians from all regions and linguistic groups have, in fact, been growing more alike, at least in aspiration if not in reality' (p. 146). His 2000 CHR forum essay (pp. 260–265 per Buckner's n. 15) is read only in its abstract: the 'limited identities' hypothesis 'has played a major role in the flowering of social history whose dominance is now being called into question by proponents of a renewed “national” approach'; the debate ignores 'the easy assumption that identities, limited or national, are essential rather than contingent', and 'it is too often forgotten that identities are multiple rather than single'. Context: Bliss's abstract (1991–92) asks historians to remember 'that their subject, after all, is Canada' and does not name Cook. Buckner (2000) writes that Cook in 1995 called the phrase 'usually attributed to Maurice Careless and I have decided that he is welcome to it!' (p. 8; Canada, Quebec and the Uses of Nationalism, 2nd ed., p. 230, unread here). Buckner then groups Bliss, Granatstein and Owram with Careless's later view that the search for limited identities had 'gone too far' (p. 9). A contribution: Cook is a root of the debate (edge 1) and a respondent who in 1993 placed himself outside both camps.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Nationalism as an object of criticism: English-Canadian nationalist intellectuals read from Canada First to the 1960s, against a 'strait-jacket identity' (1967–71)
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Cook's own text, 1967 (opening read in the OpenAlex text): Canadian Dimension's call for a union of nationalists 'of all parties' is set beside the 1874 call of 'William Foster and his exuberant young friends' (Canada First), and he answers 'Who says Canadian nationalism is difficult to define? Jobs!' (International Journal 22:4, p. 659). Two passages from 1970 are known only through quotation. Karr (Acadiensis 1989, p. 162) quotes Cook (Saturday Night, April 1970): 'Every generation of Canadian nationalist intellectuals ... seems to play the part of Sisyphus. Their permanent task is to push the millstone of Canadian nationalism up a steep mountain, only to find that it rolls back down again to await the labour of the next generation. This means that much of Canadian intellectual history sounds like a broken record'. Buckner (2000, p. 4) quotes the 1970 South Atlantic Quarterly essay, reprinted in The Maple Leaf Forever (1971, pp. 197–214): Canada 'stubbornly refuses to exchange its occasionally anarchic pluralism for a strait-jacket identity. Perhaps it is this heterogeneous pluralism itself that is the Canadian identity'. In-period reading: Karr (1989, p. 162) writes that 'it was Ramsay Cook who did so much to heighten English Canada's understanding of French-Canadian nationalism who led the anti-national crusade', and that 'While it may be easy for many to agree with Cook's belittling of this recurring obsession with national identity, there are problems inherent in extremes on both sides'. His n. 18 adds: 'while Cook is opposed to divisive nationalism, he is a centralist and appears to be searching for a cohesive, positive form of national consensus' (p. 162). Gaffield (1986, p. 143) calls him 'one of Canada's major anglophone “windows” on francophone Québec'. The Maple Leaf Forever and Canada and the French-Canadian Question (1966) are unread here. The Regenerators' place in this field is carried by edge_825.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: With Wendy Mitchinson, coedits a documentary collection on women’s place in Canadian society (The Proper Sphere, 1976).
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Existing bibliographic record confirms the editorial contribution. Does not claim sole authorship, adoption of a feminist position, influence on named historians or a reading of the full collection.
existing_incident_edges.map_label: With Wendy Mitchinson, eds., The Proper Sphere (1976)

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Careless explicitly credits Cook’s phrase and initial idea in explaining his own limited-identities programme.
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Limited Identities—Ten Years Later, opening and footnote 1. This is Careless’s own retrospective acknowledgement; he also disclaims paternity for the entire subsequent historiography. The 1969 article is not newly read, and the 1979 delivery/1980–81 issue-date qualifications remain.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Morton credits Ramsay Cook, alongside David Kwavnick, for analysis of the Task Force on National Unity report used in his 1979 address.
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Explicit own acknowledgment in note 4. Preserve Kwavnick’s shared credit; no claim that Cook supplied the entire address, endorsed its conclusions or was Morton’s teacher.

named_group_routes.relationship: Historical writing treated as a domain of English-Canadian intellectual history and its national preoccupation examined (1971–86)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: In-period evidence. Trofimenkoff (1979, p. 9, read): 'some of the people have suggested that the leit motiv of both English and French Canadian historical writing, in itself a domain of intellectual history, has been the concern for survival, a nationalist concern'; her note 4 cites Ramsay Cook's essays 'La Survivance French Canadian Style' and 'La Survivance English Canadian Style' in The Maple Leaf Forever (1971, pp. 114–40, 141–65; not read here). Karr (1989, p. 161, read) places Berger's analysis of 'the national conceptual frameworks in which professional historians functioned and wrote' among the English-Canadian intellectual historians' studies of nationalism. Berger's 1986 chapter records that 'J.M.S. Careless joined Ramsay Cook in condemning the undue emphasis on national history and unity' (p. 261, snippet view). The arrow records intellectual historians making the national tradition's writing an object of study; Berger's own contribution is the separate edge from his person entry (the Canadian persons Tier 1 revision).

named_group_routes.relationship: Staples history as a disputed Canadian antecedent of environmental history: Cook's continuity claim (1990) and Forkey's rejection (1998)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: In-period texts first; they disagree. (1) Continuity: Ramsay Cook's W. L. Morton Lecture (1990; JCS 25:4, 1990–91) claims a long Canadian concern with environment: 'In a broad sense the writing of Canadian history has always been concerned with the environment' (p. 6). Against reading the older historians as nationalists only, he writes that nationalism 'was not a full-time interest for any of them. Certainly not Harold Innis for whom the fur trade, the cod fisheries and other staple products were the real stuff of history' (p. 6). He also marks a break: 'Innis, Lower and Creighton also struggled with the question of the impact of the North American environment on European women and men', but 'for this earlier generation of historians the exploitation of the environment was accepted as natural and necessary, even though excesses might be deplored' (pp. 6–7), and 'More recent environmental historians have a different focus' (p. 7). (2) Rejection: Neil Forkey (CHR 79:1, 1998) rejects the line: 'Although the environment was an ingredient in the work of Harold A. Innis, Donald Creighton, and Arthur R.M. Lower, their studies do not serve as prototypes for Canadian environmental history'; 'In their approach, the environment exists only as a scaffolding on which human history unfolds, and not as an actor in the process' (p. 70). 'The staples model masks the essential role of social relationships and the dynamic between humans and nature', and 'More appropriate antecedents' are found in the historical geographer Andrew H. Clark (p. 71; n. 6 cites The Fur Trade in Canada and The Cod Fisheries). Classification: 'influence' here records a proposed antecedent that Canadian environmental historians disputed, not an established transmission of method; no in-period text read shows environmental historians taking up staples method, and neither position is presented as the Canadian field's. Later readings (2003–2024), labelled as such and not the evidence this edge rests on: Graeme Wynn (2003 review, p. 96) agrees that Forkey is right 'to puncture' claims 'that the staples approach represents an indigenous form of proto-environmental history'; Wynn (2004, p. 33) writes that the staples works 'focused on human uses of the environment', with 'little concern in this work for the reciprocity and mutuality of relations between people and nature'. Tina Loo (2014, p. 622) reclaims the work: 'it could be argued that some of the most influential work on the country's past was a kind of global environmental history, even if its practitioners did not call it that', naming Innis and Lower. Daniel Macfarlane's entry in NiCHE's 'Crash Course in Canadian Environmental History' (2024) holds that Innis's legacy 'still shapes many key debates and approaches in contemporary Canadian environmental history' and that, through works such as Cronon's Nature's Metropolis, the staples and metropolitan-hinterland theses 'are perhaps Canada's biggest contribution to international environmental history'. The edge records a proposed antecedent the field disagreed over; it does not say that Innis wrote environmental history or founded the field. Innis's books are unread here.

named_group_routes.relationship: The English-Canadian national tradition analysed as historiography: its major figures, their nationalism and its limits (1976; 2nd ed. 1986)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: His own statement (1976 preface, reprinted 1986; Google Books snippet view of the 1986 second edition (volume jRN6AAAAMAAJ, University of Michigan copy; preface page not reported by Google), with the 1976 edition (bix6AAAAMAAJ) checked for the preface opening and contents. Snippets are short fragments; the continuous text was not read): 'This study is an examination of aspects of English-Canadian historical thought and literature since the turn of the century. It deals with the central teachings of the major figures - George Wrong, Adam Shortt, Chester Martin, Harold Innis, Arthur Lower, Frank Underhill, Donald Creighton and William Morton - and also, in a less detailed fashion, with a more numerous group of other professional scholars who shaped the way Canadians understood their past'; 'The main emphasis is on the creative edge of historical writing and on those authors who broke the traditional patterns of interpretation'; 'Written history represents a self-conscious effort to establish the meaning of experience for the present'. The 1976 conclusion, as Allen Mills quotes it (CJPST 1977, pp. 134–137, read in full): 'Canada's historians have all been nationalists of various hues, and sometimes their judgments about what was central to the past and what was peripheral arose as much from divergent conceptions of nationality as from disagreements about interpretations of the same evidence' (p. 259; Mills p. 136). The 1986 edition replaces that conclusion with a chapter on 'the vast exfoliation of historical literature over the last twenty years' (preface to the second edition). There 'A few historians in the sixties, moreover, subjected the tradition in which they had grown up to searching criticism. J.M.S. Careless joined Ramsay Cook in condemning the undue emphasis on national history and unity' (p. 261), and he quotes Careless (1969) that the 'nation-building approach' 'neglects and obscures even while it explains and illuminates' (p. 262); social history's 'initial impact was to magnify the diversity of Canadian history' (p. 298). In-period reception. Mills: the book 'makes a substantial contribution to the intellectual history of English Canada' and 'is really about' its eight 'superluminaries' (p. 135); 'his description of all Canadian historians as nationalists places much too much weight on that over-used term', since they 'have very different conceptions of the nation that is to survive' (p. 136); but 'Berger's claim that Canadian historians have been generally unconcerned to explore the group loyalties of class, region, culture and family is unimpeachable' (pp. 136–137). Terry Cook (Archivaria 5, 1977–78, pp. 198–203, read in full) calls it 'a remarkably subtle analysis of major trends in Canadian historiography' that 'transcends historiography to become an intellectual history of English Canada in the twentieth century' (p. 202). (Cook gives the 'nation-building' passage at p. 263 of the 1976 edition without naming Careless; the 1986 text attributes it to Careless.) Karr (1989, p. 161): 'As a sequel he analysed the national conceptual frameworks in which professional historians functioned and wrote.' The French-Canadian limit is his own choice, explained in the preface: 'two language traditions have, in historical thought as well as in other non-political spheres, occasionally touched and intersected, but in general they have been preoccupied with the backgrounds of two rather different “nations”', and a comparison 'must rest on preliminary appraisals of the individual traditions'; 'the two traditions of historical writing flowed in separate channels' (p. 181). Ronald Rudin (1997; snippet view) shares 'Berger's belief that historical writing can “reveal a good deal about the intellectual climate in which it was composed”' but does 'not accept his assumption, implicit in Writing of Canadian History, that historians across the twentieth century have been united by their search for the truth' (p. 4), and finds that 'Berger failed, however, to consider the way in which Groulx had, by the 1930s, altered his view of the Dollard affair' (p. 58). Gregory Kealey (1982, reprinted 1995; snippet view) notes that the Marxist Stanley Ryerson 'was not considered for systematic evaluation in The Writing of Canadian History' (1995, p. 84), while finding 'little to argue with' in Berger's 1986 summary of the labour-history debate (1995, p. 18).

named_group_routes.relationship: Cook's phrase 'limited identities' made a programme for Canadian history (1969), and region read through the metropolitan systems that structure it (1979–89)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: The 1969 article (CHR 50:1, pp. 1–10) is unread here; its wording comes from two witnesses. Buckner (Acadiensis 30:1, 2000, p. 4, read): Careless 'insisted that the “Canadian experience” must be “discerned and defined” through the “limited identities of region, culture and class referred to by Professor Cook”', and concluded that 'the whole may indeed be greater than the sum of its parts, producing through its internal relationships some sort of common Canadianism'. Careless himself, in 'Limited Identities — Ten Years Later' (Manitoba History no. 1, 1981; a lecture given in 1979; read in full, web text without page numbers), summarises the article as noting that these identities 'had tended to bulk larger for Canadians in their history than any identification with overall national patterns of values and attitudes', and quotes its p. 10: 'by pursuing a line largely of sociocultural inquiry, one may hope to uncover satisfactions in the limited identities ... which have added up to some positive balance of satisfaction with Canada itself'. The phrase is Cook's: Careless wrote that he 'did not invent the term “limited identity”, but acquired it from an article by Ramsay Cook, cited in my own article — which was thus essentially a commentary on his initial idea' (1981, n. 1); Buckner (p. 4) says Cook 'coined' it and Careless 'popularized' it. This edge carries Careless's programme, not the coinage. The 1981 lecture joins it to metropolitanism: regionalist historians often present 'an over-simple dichotomy' between a metropolitan central Canada and their own region, whereas 'regions are structured into metropolitan systems both within and beyond their territories'; 'Metropolitanism is not the antithesis of regionalism. Each is inherent in the other'. Frontier and Metropolis (1989) is unread; Rick Szostak's review (Journal of Economic History 50:2, 1990, pp. 499–501, read) reports that in it 'Cities become the foci of regional identity' and that Atlantic Canada 'develops a regional identity despite having no one dominant metropolis' (p. 500). In-period reception: the 1973 bibliography by Hann, Kealey, Kealey and Warrian opened with 'For some time J. M. S. Careless has called for ... a historical appreciation of the varieties of “limited identities” that constitute Canada' (as Careless quotes it in 1981; a quoted-in witness). Criticism: Buckner (2000, p. 10) answers critics who treat regional studies as, 'as Careless and Granatstein seem to believe, a construct designed to justify the dismantling of the Canadian state'; Robert Irwin (Journal of Canadian Studies 32:3, 1997; abstract only) argues that prairie identity 'must be understood as an autonomous layer of consciousness rather than a “limited identity” within a national consciousness'; Szostak found the book 'descriptive rather than analytical' and expected readers to be 'left unconvinced' (p. 500). Buckner (p. 5) also notes the different motives: Cook and Careless embraced the concept partly in response to Quebec separatism, Atlantic historians for other reasons. edge_805 and edge_814 stay as group-level arrows.

named_group_routes.relationship: Limited identities and regional explanation criticised from a class standpoint: 'limited identities' as 'neither "limited" nor analytically separable' (1978), region as 'the crucial variable' 'increasingly misplaced' and western exceptionalism overstated (1981), and the 1919 revolt as 'national in character' (1984)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: His own words, in period. Acadiensis 7:2 (1978), read at pp. 116–117 and 134–135: Cook and Careless 'called for a turn away from nation and politics' toward 'region, ethnicity and class' (p. 116, citing Cook 1967 and Careless 1969); 'The call for attention to "limited identities" was the death-knell of Laurentianism' (p. 117); 'The long-overdue insertion of a class analysis into Canadian historical writing already promises overviews which transcend the refreshing and liberating pluralism of the 1960s calls for attention to region, ethnicity and class. It should be increasingly clear, however, that these so-called "limited identities" are neither "limited" nor analytically separable. No historical notion of class (and there can be no other useful notion) can fail to incorporate ethnicity and place' (p. 135). Labour/Le Travailleur 7 (1981), read in full: 'NONE CAN DENY the importance of regional differences … Yet the increasing emphasis placed on "region" as the crucial variable which explains sundry problems of Canadian development seems increasingly misplaced', citing Westfall on the regional interpretation standing 'the old nationalist history on its head' (p. 74); before the 1890s 'there was not one Canadian working class but many' (p. 75); accounts of western workers are shaped by 'a strong sense of western exceptionalism', and 'the rather easy assumptions of a unique western working-class militancy have been overstated', with n. 25: 'David Bercuson has been most guilty of this' (p. 76); 'Canadian historians have come to believe everything was different everywhere … This celebration of region has fit very well with the general direction of Canadian political life in the last decade. Surely the time has come to begin to reflect on region in a critical way' (p. 76); his remedy is not 'A return to an old national history? No, of course not, but rather the consideration on a national scale of the particular class experiences of Canadian workers in local and regional contexts which adds up to something more than local and regional exceptionalism' (p. 77). '1919: The Canadian Labour Revolt', Labour/Le Travail 13 (1984), pp. 11–44, read at pp. 11–17: 'These examples are intended simply to demonstrate that the revolt was national in character and that its seeds were not rooted in any unique regional fermentation. The "radical" west and the conservative east have become sorry shibboleths of Canadian historiography'; 'the similarities of struggle begin to outweigh the initial impression of regional particularism' (p. 15). Qualifications kept: he grants 'the importance of regional differences' (1981, p. 74) and calls Maritime underdevelopment real (pp. 75–76); the 1978 sentence welcomes the 1960s pluralism as 'refreshing and liberating' before arguing that class analysis transcends it. In-period reading: Morton (2000, p. 25, read) credits Kealey, Palmer, Heron, Hann and others with bringing labour history 'back from superstructure, politics, and the exceptionalism of Western Canada to regions that had been largely neglected by their predecessors: Ontario and the Maritimes'. No reply by Bercuson to the 1981 or 1984 regional argument was checked. Distinct from Cook's 1977–83 critique of regionalism (edge from ramsay_cook to cdn_regional), which doubts region as a unit; Kealey's subordinates it to class and national-scale capitalism.

named_group_routes.relationship: Careless's second thoughts about the 'flood' of regional, cultural and class writing (1979 lecture) read as a reaction reasserting 'a "positive" unifying national history' (1988); a decade earlier the working-class bibliography Kealey co-compiled had invoked Careless's limited identities (1973)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Kealey's words, in period. Introduction to Class, Gender, and Region: Essays in Canadian Historical Sociology (St. John's: CCLH, 1988; reprint of a Canadian Journal of Sociology special issue), pp. 1–7, read in the AU Press PDF: 'The degree to which reaction has re-emerged to reassert the need for a "positive" unifying national history can be seen by contrasting the views of J.M.S. Careless in 1969 and in 1980. In 1969, Careless enthusiastically embraced Ramsay Cook's earlier call for the study of region, class, and ethnicity … By 1980, however, he had serious doubts' (p. 2); he quotes Careless's farmer 'in the midst of the flood' and answers: 'As I hope this volume suggests, such plaintiff [sic] Toronto cries to date have not been able to dam the flood of critical scholarship on class, gender, and region' (p. 3). 'The impatience mentioned by Berger and articulated by Careless addresses itself as much to this regional revolt as it does to writings concerned with class and gender' (p. 5). Careless's text, re-read (Manitoba History no. 1, web text, unpaginated; the 1979 Jackson lecture, cited by Kealey as 1980): 'there has been a massive outpouring … on class disparities and stresses and such things as national concerns are by and large passed over or discounted. In this situation, I feel a little like the farmer in the midst of a flood'. Qualifications kept: Careless continues, 'there are reasons why I do not really feel as bad as the foregoing might suggest', calls working-class history 'one of the most active and productive areas' of the study of limited identities, and asks that class identities 'be treated in their national scope', a point close to Kealey's own (1981, p. 77). Kealey's 'reaction' is his reading of the lecture. Earlier connection: Careless (1979) quotes the introduction to Primary Sources in Canadian Working-Class History (1973, p. 11), compiled by Hann, Gregory and Linda Kealey and Warrian: 'For some time J. M. S. Careless has called for … a historical appreciation of the varieties of "limited identities" that constitute Canada'. Kealey (1981, p. 68) says that statement was 'drafted by Russell Hann'. No reply by Careless was checked. Related: edge_954 (Careless → who_killed_debate) records the fragmentation worry this passage voices; pe138_kealey_rel_02 records Kealey's separate critique of limited identities from a class standpoint (1978).
